Prompt: Name a bone of the neurocranium.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Frontal bone [Common, 25m] (aliases: frontal); Parietal bone [Common, 25m] (aliases: parietal); Temporal bone [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: temporal); Occipital bone [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: occipital); Sphenoid bone [Rare, 50m] (aliases: sphenoid); Ethmoid bone [Rare, 50m] (aliases: ethmoid)
Hint: Think of the eight cranial bones, counting paired bones.
Explanation: The neurocranium encloses and protects the brain. Its eight bones are the frontal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid bones plus paired parietal and temporal bones.

Prompt: Name a facial bone.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Mandible [Common, 25m]; Maxilla [Common, 25m] (aliases: maxillary bone); Zygomatic bone [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: cheekbone); Nasal bone [Uncommon, 25m]; Lacrimal bone [Rare, 50m]; Palatine bone [Rare, 50m]; Vomer [Deep Cut, 90m]; Inferior nasal concha [Deep Cut, 90m] (aliases: inferior turbinate)
Hint: Think jaw, cheek, nose, palate, and orbit.
Explanation: The facial skeleton forms the framework of the face, orbits, nasal cavity and jaws. Most facial bones are paired; the mandible and vomer are unpaired.

Prompt: Name a major cranial suture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Coronal suture [Common, 10m]; Sagittal suture [Common, 10m]; Lambdoid suture [Uncommon, 25m]; Squamous suture [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: squamosal suture)
Hint: One joins the two parietal bones.
Explanation: Cranial sutures are fibrous joints between skull bones: coronal joins frontal to parietals; sagittal joins parietals; lambdoid joins parietals to occipital; squamous joins temporal to parietal.

Prompt: Name a feature of the frontal bone shown in lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Glabella [Common, 10m]; Frontal sinus [Common, 10m] (aliases: frontal sinuses); Anterior cranial fossa [Uncommon, 25m]; Roof of orbit [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: orbital roof)
Explanation: The frontal bone contributes to the forehead, anterior cranial fossa and roof of each orbit. The glabella lies between the eyebrows, and the frontal sinuses are air-filled spaces within the bone.

Prompt: Name a landmark of the temporal bone shown in lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Mastoid process [Common, 10m]; Styloid process [Common, 10m]; External acoustic meatus [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: external auditory canal); Mandibular fossa [Uncommon, 25m]; Zygomatic arch [Rare, 50m]; Middle cranial fossa [Rare, 50m]
Explanation: The temporal bone forms part of the lateral skull and cranial base. Its external acoustic meatus leads toward the tympanic membrane; the mandibular fossa articulates with the mandible at the TMJ.

Prompt: Name a feature of the sphenoid bone shown in lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Sella turcica [Common, 10m] (aliases: hypophyseal fossa); Greater wing [Common, 10m]; Lesser wing [Uncommon, 25m]; Pterygoid process [Uncommon, 25m]; Optic canal [Rare, 50m] (aliases: optic foramen); Superior orbital fissure [Rare, 50m]
Hint: Think saddle-shaped pituitary seat and orbital openings.
Explanation: The sphenoid is a central cranial-base bone. Its sella turcica houses the pituitary gland, while its wings, pterygoid processes, optic canal and superior orbital fissure contribute to cranial and orbital anatomy.

Prompt: Name a feature of the ethmoid bone shown in lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Cribriform plate [Common, 10m]; Crista galli [Common, 10m]; Perpendicular plate [Uncommon, 25m]; Superior nasal concha [Uncommon, 25m]; Middle nasal concha [Rare, 50m]
Hint: Think nasal septum and olfactory roof.
Explanation: The ethmoid contributes to the nasal septum and lateral nasal wall. Olfactory nerve filaments pass through the cribriform plate; the crista galli anchors the falx cerebri.

Prompt: Name a landmark of the mandible shown in lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Body of mandible [Common, 10m]; Ramus of mandible [Common, 10m] (aliases: mandibular ramus); Mandibular angle [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: angle of mandible); Mandibular notch [Uncommon, 25m]; Coronoid process [Rare, 50m]; Mandibular condyle [Rare, 50m] (aliases: condylar process); Mental foramen [Deep Cut, 90m]; Mandibular foramen [Deep Cut, 90m]
Hint: Think body, ramus, processes and foramina.
Explanation: The mandibular body forms the chin and lower dental arch; the ramus ascends to the coronoid and condylar processes. The mandibular and mental foramina transmit branches of the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle.

Prompt: Which suture joins the two parietal bones?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Sagittal suture [Fixed, 25m]
Hint: It runs along the superior midline.
Explanation: The sagittal suture lies in the midline between the right and left parietal bones. The coronal suture instead separates frontal from parietal bones.

Prompt: Which skull bone contains the foramen magnum?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Occipital bone [Fixed, 25m]
Explanation: The foramen magnum is the large opening in the occipital bone through which the medulla continues as the spinal cord, with associated vessels and other structures.

Prompt: Name a facial expression muscle from Head I.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Orbicularis oculi [Common, 25m]; Orbicularis oris [Common, 25m]; Buccinator [Uncommon, 25m]; Zygomaticus [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: zygomaticus major, zygomaticus minor); Risorius [Rare, 50m]; Frontalis [Rare, 50m] (aliases: frontal belly of epicranius); Occipitalis [Deep Cut, 90m] (aliases: occipital belly of epicranius)
Hint: Think eyelids, lips, cheek and scalp.
Explanation: Facial expression muscles insert into skin or adjacent soft tissue and produce movements such as closing the eyes or lips and moving the cheeks. Their motor innervation is supplied by CN VII.

Prompt: Name a muscle of mastication.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Masseter [Common, 25m]; Temporalis [Common, 25m]; Medial pterygoid [Uncommon, 25m]; Lateral pterygoid [Uncommon, 25m]
Explanation: The four principal muscles of mastication move the mandible. Masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid primarily elevate it; lateral pterygoid contributes to protrusion and opening.

Prompt: Which cranial nerve provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Mandibular division of trigeminal nerve [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: CN V3, V3, mandibular nerve)
Explanation: Motor fibers of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve supply the muscles of mastication. V1 and V2 are sensory divisions.

Prompt: Which cranial nerve innervates the muscles of facial expression?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Facial nerve [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: CN VII, cranial nerve 7, seventh cranial nerve)
Hint: Do not confuse facial expression with mastication.
Explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) provides branchial motor supply to muscles of facial expression. CN V mainly provides general facial sensation and V3 also innervates mastication muscles.

Prompt: Name an extraocular muscle.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Medial rectus [Common, 25m]; Lateral rectus [Common, 25m]; Superior rectus [Uncommon, 25m]; Inferior rectus [Uncommon, 25m]; Superior oblique [Rare, 50m]; Inferior oblique [Rare, 50m]
Explanation: The four rectus and two oblique muscles move the eyeball. Their innervation follows LR6 SO4, with the remaining four muscles supplied by CN III.

Prompt: Which nerve innervates the lateral rectus?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Abducens nerve [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: CN VI, cranial nerve 6, sixth cranial nerve)
Explanation: The lateral rectus abducts the eye and is innervated by CN VI (abducens). Remember LR6: lateral rectus, cranial nerve six.

Prompt: Which nerve innervates the superior oblique?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Trochlear nerve [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: CN IV, cranial nerve 4, fourth cranial nerve)
Explanation: The superior oblique is supplied by CN IV (trochlear). Its actions include intorsion, depression and abduction depending on eye position.

Prompt: Name an extraocular muscle innervated by CN III.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Medial rectus [Common, 10m]; Superior rectus [Common, 10m]; Inferior rectus [Uncommon, 25m]; Inferior oblique [Uncommon, 25m]
Explanation: CN III supplies medial, superior and inferior rectus and inferior oblique. Lateral rectus is supplied by CN VI and superior oblique by CN IV.

Prompt: Which muscle primarily abducts the eye?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Lateral rectus [Fixed, 25m]
Hint: The lateral rectus moves the eye laterally.
Explanation: Lateral rectus pulls the globe laterally, producing abduction. Medial rectus instead adducts the eye.

Prompt: Name a meningeal layer surrounding the brain.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Dura mater [Common, 25m] (aliases: dura); Arachnoid mater [Common, 25m] (aliases: arachnoid); Pia mater [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: pia)
Explanation: The meninges comprise outer dura mater, middle arachnoid mater and inner pia mater. CSF circulates in the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia.

Prompt: Name a dural reflection shown in Head I.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Falx cerebri [Common, 10m]; Tentorium cerebelli [Common, 10m]; Falx cerebelli [Uncommon, 25m]
Hint: The falx and tentorium are folds of dura.
Explanation: Dural reflections partition and support parts of the brain. Falx cerebri separates cerebral hemispheres; tentorium cerebelli separates cerebrum from cerebellum; falx cerebelli separates cerebellar hemispheres.

Prompt: Which structure produces most cerebrospinal fluid?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Choroid plexus [Fixed, 25m]
Hint: The lecture describes ependymal cells and permeable capillaries.
Explanation: The choroid plexus in the ventricles produces most cerebrospinal fluid by secretion from specialized epithelial cells associated with capillaries.

Prompt: Name a major subdivision of the developing brain listed in Head I.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Telencephalon [Common, 10m]; Diencephalon [Common, 10m]; Mesencephalon [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: midbrain); Metencephalon [Uncommon, 25m]; Myelencephalon [Rare, 50m]
Explanation: The secondary brain vesicles are telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon and myelencephalon. Together they develop into forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain structures.

Prompt: Name a structure belonging to the diencephalon.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Thalamus [Common, 10m]; Hypothalamus [Common, 10m]; Epithalamus [Uncommon, 25m]
Hint: Three structures named on the brain organization slide.
Explanation: The diencephalon includes thalamic and hypothalamic regions as well as the epithalamus. It is part of the forebrain, distinct from the cerebral hemispheres of the telencephalon.

Prompt: Which developmental division gives rise to the pons and cerebellum?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Metencephalon [Fixed, 25m]
Explanation: The metencephalon develops into the pons and cerebellum. The myelencephalon develops into the medulla oblongata.

Prompt: Name a paranasal sinus.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Frontal sinus [Common, 25m]; Maxillary sinus [Common, 25m]; Ethmoidal air cells [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: ethmoid sinus, ethmoidal sinus); Sphenoid sinus [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: sphenoidal sinus)
Hint: Four groups surround the nasal cavity.
Explanation: Paranasal sinuses are air-filled spaces in the frontal, maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid bones. They communicate with the nasal cavity.

Prompt: Name a component of the nasal septum.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Septal cartilage [Common, 10m] (aliases: quadrangular cartilage); Perpendicular plate of ethmoid [Common, 10m] (aliases: perpendicular plate); Vomer [Uncommon, 25m]
Explanation: The nasal septum is formed by septal cartilage anteriorly, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid superiorly and the vomer posteroinferiorly.

Prompt: Name a nasal concha shown in the lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Inferior nasal concha [Common, 25m] (aliases: inferior turbinate); Middle nasal concha [Common, 25m] (aliases: middle turbinate); Superior nasal concha [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: superior turbinate)
Explanation: Superior and middle nasal conchae are parts of the ethmoid bone; the inferior nasal concha is a separate bone. Conchae increase nasal surface area and influence airflow.

Prompt: Name a structure forming the floor of the nasal cavity.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Maxilla [Common, 10m] (aliases: maxillary bone, palatine process of maxilla); Palatine bone [Common, 10m] (aliases: horizontal plate of palatine bone)
Hint: The floor is the hard palate.
Explanation: The hard palate forms the floor of the nasal cavity and roof of the oral cavity. Its bony parts include the palatine processes of maxillae and horizontal plates of palatine bones.

Prompt: Which bone forms the cribriform plate at the roof of the nasal cavity?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Ethmoid bone [Fixed, 25m]
Explanation: The cribriform plate belongs to the ethmoid bone and forms part of the nasal roof. Olfactory fibers traverse its tiny foramina.

Prompt: Name an external ear landmark labeled on the lecture diagram.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Helix [Common, 25m]; Antihelix [Common, 25m]; Tragus [Uncommon, 25m]; Antitragus [Uncommon, 25m]; Lobule [Rare, 50m] (aliases: earlobe); Concha [Rare, 50m]; Scapha [Deep Cut, 90m]; Triangular fossa [Deep Cut, 90m]; Intertragic notch [Deep Cut, 90m]
Hint: Think ridges, depressions, and the earlobe.
Explanation: The auricle, also called the pinna, collects sound. Its named surface landmarks include helix, antihelix, tragus, antitragus, concha, lobule and adjacent fossae/notches.

Prompt: Name an auditory ossicle.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Malleus [Common, 25m] (aliases: hammer); Incus [Common, 25m] (aliases: anvil); Stapes [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: stirrup)
Explanation: The malleus, incus and stapes form an ossicular chain that transmits vibrations from the tympanic membrane toward the oval window of the inner ear.

Prompt: Name a component of the inner ear shown in the diagram.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Cochlea [Common, 10m]; Semicircular canals [Common, 10m] (aliases: semicircular ducts); Vestibule [Uncommon, 25m]
Explanation: The cochlea is associated with hearing; the vestibule and semicircular canals participate in balance and detection of head movement.

Prompt: Which tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Pharyngotympanic tube [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: auditory tube, Eustachian tube)
Explanation: The pharyngotympanic (auditory/Eustachian) tube connects the middle ear with the nasopharynx and helps equalize air pressure across the tympanic membrane.

Prompt: Name a branch of CN VIII shown in the ear diagram.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Vestibular nerve [Common, 10m]; Cochlear nerve [Common, 10m]
Explanation: CN VIII has cochlear fibers for hearing and vestibular fibers for balance. Both components travel through the internal acoustic meatus.

Prompt: Name a major salivary gland.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Parotid gland [Common, 25m] (aliases: parotid); Submandibular gland [Common, 25m] (aliases: submandibular); Sublingual gland [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: sublingual)
Hint: There are three paired major glands.
Explanation: The three paired major salivary glands are parotid, submandibular and sublingual. Their ducts deliver saliva to the oral cavity.

Prompt: Name a type of permanent tooth.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Incisor [Common, 25m]; Canine [Common, 25m] (aliases: cuspid); Premolar [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: bicuspid); Molar [Uncommon, 25m]
Explanation: Adult permanent teeth are categorized as incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, premolars for crushing and molars for grinding.

Prompt: Name an anatomical structure of the oral cavity labeled on the lecture slide.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Hard palate [Common, 10m]; Soft palate [Common, 10m]; Uvula [Uncommon, 25m]; Tongue [Uncommon, 25m]; Lingual frenulum [Rare, 50m]; Labial frenulum [Rare, 50m]; Palatine tonsil [Deep Cut, 90m]; Gingiva [Deep Cut, 90m] (aliases: gingivae, gums); Vestibule [Deep Cut, 90m]; Fauces [Deep Cut, 90m]
Hint: Look at the oral cavity diagram.
Explanation: The oral cavity includes the palate, tongue, gingiva, vestibule and openings toward the oropharynx. The uvula hangs from the soft palate; the fauces form the passage to the oropharynx.

Prompt: How many permanent teeth are in a complete adult dentition?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: 32 [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: thirty two, thirty-two)
Explanation: A complete permanent dentition has 32 teeth: in each quadrant, two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars.

Prompt: Name a structure of the tongue shown in Head II.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Dorsum of tongue [Common, 10m] (aliases: dorsum); Lingual frenulum [Common, 10m] (aliases: frenulum of tongue); Lingual papillae [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: papillae)
Hint: Think upper surface and underside attachments.
Explanation: The dorsum is the superior tongue surface; lingual papillae contribute to its texture and some house taste buds. The lingual frenulum anchors its inferior surface to the floor of the mouth.

Prompt: Name an artery supplying the brain in the Head II lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Internal carotid artery [Common, 25m] (aliases: ICA); Vertebral artery [Common, 25m]; Basilar artery [Uncommon, 25m]; Anterior cerebral artery [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: ACA); Posterior cerebral artery [Rare, 50m] (aliases: PCA); Anterior communicating artery [Rare, 50m] (aliases: ACom, ACoA); Posterior communicating artery [Deep Cut, 90m] (aliases: PCom, PCoA)
Explanation: The brain receives blood from internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. Vertebral arteries unite into the basilar artery; cerebral and communicating arteries distribute and connect flow at the base of the brain.

Prompt: Name an artery in the Circle of Willis.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Anterior cerebral artery [Common, 10m] (aliases: ACA); Anterior communicating artery [Common, 10m] (aliases: ACom, ACoA); Internal carotid artery [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: ICA); Posterior communicating artery [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: PCom, PCoA); Posterior cerebral artery [Rare, 50m] (aliases: PCA)
Hint: The MCA is not part of the circle.
Explanation: The cerebral arterial circle links anterior circulation from internal carotids with posterior circulation via posterior cerebral arteries and communicating arteries. The middle cerebral artery is not a ring component.

Prompt: Which artery is formed by the union of the vertebral arteries?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Basilar artery [Fixed, 25m]
Explanation: The right and left vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery on the ventral brainstem. The basilar artery ultimately divides into posterior cerebral arteries.

Prompt: Which artery connects the two anterior cerebral arteries?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Anterior communicating artery [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: ACom, ACoA)
Explanation: The anterior communicating artery bridges the left and right anterior cerebral arteries, completing the anterior part of the cerebral arterial circle.

Prompt: Which artery connects the internal carotid system with the posterior cerebral artery?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Posterior communicating artery [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: PCom, PCoA)
Explanation: Each posterior communicating artery connects an internal carotid artery to the ipsilateral posterior cerebral artery, linking anterior and posterior circulations.

Prompt: Name a cranial nerve that controls eye movement.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Oculomotor nerve [Common, 25m] (aliases: CN III, cranial nerve 3); Trochlear nerve [Common, 25m] (aliases: CN IV, cranial nerve 4); Abducens nerve [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: CN VI, cranial nerve 6)
Explanation: CN III innervates most extraocular muscles; CN IV supplies superior oblique and CN VI supplies lateral rectus. This is summarized by LR6 SO4, all others III.

Prompt: Which cranial nerve transmits olfactory information?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Olfactory nerve [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: CN I, cranial nerve 1)
Explanation: Olfactory nerve fibers (CN I) transmit smell from olfactory epithelium through foramina of the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb.

Prompt: Which cranial nerve is responsible for tongue motor movements?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Hypoglossal nerve [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: CN XII, cranial nerve 12)
Explanation: CN XII supplies motor innervation to intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles. Palatoglossus is the major exception, supplied by CN X.

Prompt: Name a cranial nerve that traverses the jugular foramen.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Glossopharyngeal nerve [Common, 10m] (aliases: CN IX, cranial nerve 9); Vagus nerve [Common, 10m] (aliases: CN X, cranial nerve 10); Accessory nerve [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: CN XI, cranial nerve 11)
Explanation: CN IX, X and XI traverse the jugular foramen. CN XII exits through the separate hypoglossal canal.

Prompt: Which cranial nerve passes through the hypoglossal canal?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Hypoglossal nerve [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: CN XII, cranial nerve 12)
Hint: The canal shares the nerve name.
Explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone and supplies most tongue muscles.

Prompt: Name a direct branch of the aortic arch listed in lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Brachiocephalic trunk [Common, 25m] (aliases: brachiocephalic artery); Left common carotid artery [Common, 25m] (aliases: left common carotid); Left subclavian artery [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: left subclavian)
Explanation: The aortic arch gives off three principal branches: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian. The brachiocephalic trunk then supplies the right common carotid and right subclavian.

Prompt: Name a branch of the external carotid artery.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Facial artery [Common, 10m]; Lingual artery [Common, 10m]; Superior thyroid artery [Uncommon, 25m]; Maxillary artery [Uncommon, 25m]; Superficial temporal artery [Rare, 50m]; Occipital artery [Rare, 50m]; Posterior auricular artery [Deep Cut, 90m]; Ascending pharyngeal artery [Deep Cut, 90m]
Hint: Think thyroid, tongue, face, pharynx and scalp.
Explanation: The external carotid supplies structures of the face, scalp and neck via eight principal branches: superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary and superficial temporal.

Prompt: Name one terminal branch of the common carotid artery.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Internal carotid artery [Common, 25m] (aliases: ICA); External carotid artery [Common, 25m] (aliases: ECA)
Hint: The carotid bifurcation has two branches.
Explanation: Each common carotid bifurcates into internal and external carotid arteries. The internal carotid primarily supplies intracranial structures; the external carotid supplies much of the head and neck outside the cranium.

Prompt: Name a jugular vein labeled in the Neck lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Internal jugular vein [Common, 25m] (aliases: IJV, IJ); External jugular vein [Common, 25m] (aliases: EJV, EJ)
Explanation: Internal jugular veins drain much of the brain and deep head/neck; external jugular veins drain superficial regions. The Neck lecture labels both.

Prompt: Which aortic arch branch gives rise to the right common carotid artery?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Brachiocephalic trunk [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: brachiocephalic artery)
Hint: This trunk also gives rise to the right subclavian.
Explanation: The brachiocephalic trunk arises from the aortic arch and divides into right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid arises directly from the arch.

Prompt: Which carotid artery supplies the brain rather than giving off neck branches?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Internal carotid artery [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: ICA)
Hint: The other carotid supplies face and neck.
Explanation: The internal carotid enters the cranial cavity and contributes to cerebral circulation. Unlike the external carotid, it normally gives no branches in the neck.

Prompt: Name a neck muscle explicitly named on the Neck lecture slide.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Sternocleidomastoid [Common, 25m] (aliases: SCM); Scalenes [Common, 25m] (aliases: scalene muscles)
Explanation: Sternocleidomastoid rotates and flexes the head/neck; scalene muscles assist lateral neck flexion and can elevate upper ribs during inspiration.

Prompt: Name a pharyngeal constrictor muscle.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Superior pharyngeal constrictor [Common, 10m]; Middle pharyngeal constrictor [Common, 10m]; Inferior pharyngeal constrictor [Uncommon, 25m]
Hint: There are superior, middle and inferior constrictors.
Explanation: Superior, middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictors sequentially constrict the pharynx during swallowing, propelling a food bolus toward the esophagus.

Prompt: Which muscle is commonly abbreviated SCM?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Sternocleidomastoid [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: SCM)
Explanation: SCM stands for sternocleidomastoid, a prominent superficial neck muscle extending between sternum/clavicle and mastoid process.

Prompt: Name a suprahyoid muscle labeled on the Neck muscle diagram.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Digastric [Common, 10m]; Mylohyoid [Common, 10m]; Stylohyoid [Uncommon, 25m]; Geniohyoid [Uncommon, 25m]
Explanation: Suprahyoid muscles lie above the hyoid and help elevate it or the floor of the mouth during swallowing; the diagram identifies digastric, mylohyoid, stylohyoid and geniohyoid.

Prompt: Name an infrahyoid muscle labeled on the Neck muscle diagram.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Sternohyoid [Common, 10m]; Omohyoid [Common, 10m]; Sternothyroid [Uncommon, 25m]; Thyrohyoid [Uncommon, 25m]
Explanation: Infrahyoid strap muscles lie below the hyoid and generally depress or stabilize it and the larynx; the diagram labels sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid and thyrohyoid.

Prompt: Name a region of the pharynx.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Nasopharynx [Common, 25m]; Oropharynx [Common, 25m]; Laryngopharynx [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: hypopharynx)
Explanation: The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity, the oropharynx behind the mouth and the laryngopharynx behind the laryngeal inlet.

Prompt: Name an unpaired laryngeal cartilage.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Thyroid cartilage [Common, 25m]; Cricoid cartilage [Common, 25m]; Epiglottic cartilage [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: epiglottis, epiglottal cartilage)
Explanation: The unpaired laryngeal cartilages are thyroid, cricoid and epiglottic. They provide the larger structural framework of the larynx.

Prompt: Name a paired laryngeal cartilage.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Arytenoid cartilage [Common, 10m]; Corniculate cartilage [Common, 10m]; Cuneiform cartilage [Uncommon, 25m]
Explanation: The paired arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages support the laryngeal inlet and vocal-fold mechanism. Arytenoid movement is important in vocal-fold positioning.

Prompt: Name a function of the larynx described in lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Voice production [Common, 10m] (aliases: phonation); Maintain a patent airway [Common, 10m] (aliases: airway patency); Route air and food into proper channels [Uncommon, 25m] (aliases: airway protection)
Explanation: The larynx maintains an open airway, protects the lower airway during swallowing and generates voice through vocal-fold vibration.

Prompt: Name a laryngeal membrane or ligament labeled in the lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Thyrohyoid membrane [Common, 10m]; Cricothyroid ligament [Common, 10m] (aliases: median cricothyroid ligament)
Hint: One spans thyroid to hyoid, another thyroid to cricoid.
Explanation: The thyrohyoid membrane spans hyoid to thyroid cartilage; the cricothyroid membrane/ligament lies between thyroid and cricoid cartilages and is relevant to emergency airway access.

Prompt: Which nerve innervates most intrinsic laryngeal muscles?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Recurrent laryngeal nerve [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: RLN)
Hint: The lecture labels the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates nearly all intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Cricothyroid is the key exception and is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

Prompt: Which bone supports the larynx without articulating directly with another bone?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Hyoid bone [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: hyoid)
Explanation: The hyoid bone is suspended by muscles and ligaments rather than directly articulating with another bone; it supports tongue and laryngeal movements.

Prompt: Name a structure near the laryngeal inlet labeled in the Neck lecture.
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Aryepiglottic fold [Common, 10m]; Piriform recess [Common, 10m] (aliases: piriform fossa, pyriform recess)
Explanation: The aryepiglottic folds outline the laryngeal inlet. Piriform recesses lie lateral to the inlet and help channel swallowed material toward the esophagus.

Prompt: Which ligament or membrane is traversed in a cricothyrotomy?
Accepted canonical answers and rarity/de: Cricothyroid membrane [Fixed, 25m] (aliases: median cricothyroid ligament, cricothyroid ligament)
